title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Stripped Payloads
shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Stripped Payloads
summary: Stripped payloads are executables or scripts from which the human readable scaffolding has been removed before delivery. Compilers and linkers normally leave function names, symbol tables, section headers, and debug references that tell an analyst what the code is called and how it is arranged; strip options and build flags delete that material, leaving machine instructions with almost no labels. Interpreted payloads receive the equivalent treatment when variable names are shortened and strings are encoded or removed, and some platforms ship a compiled script format that cannot be read back into source at all. The practical result is slower analysis: control flow and behaviour can still be followed, but routines must be named by hand and dynamic tracing used. A payload with no symbols and no useful strings is a deliberate choice, not an accident.

beginner.definition: Programs usually carry small labels that help people read them. The labels include names of functions and variables. Stripping means removing those labels before sending the program out. The program still runs exactly the same, but the reading aids are gone.
beginner.whyItMatters: Analysts read those labels to understand quickly what a program does. Without them, the work takes much longer and costs more time. Attackers strip their tools to slow down investigation and response. Some script formats cannot be turned back into readable text at all. Slower analysis gives the attacker more time to keep working.
howItWorks: The attacker builds the program or script as usual.
They use a tool option or a separate utility that deletes names and symbol information.
Strings that describe purpose, such as messages or file paths, may also be removed or hidden.
For scripts, they shorten variable names and encode text so the meaning is lost.
They may convert the script into a compiled form that cannot be read back into source.
The payload is delivered and runs normally, but explaining it by reading is much harder.
beginner.example: Imagine a toolbox where every drawer label has been scraped off. All the tools are still there and still work. You must open every drawer and test each tool to learn what it does. Stripping a program removes the labels in the same way. The working parts stay in place, but reading becomes slow.
takeaways: Stripping removes human readable labels but not the behaviour of the program.
Missing symbols and useful strings are themselves worth noting as a clue.
Dynamic tracing and sandbox runs recover behaviour when static reading stalls.

objectives: Explain what symbols and strings are and why analysts rely on them.
Describe how executables and scripts are stripped before delivery.
Explain why stripped payloads slow down investigation and response.
Identify file properties that indicate a payload has been stripped.
Describe how dynamic analysis compensates for missing labels.
